Latent Structure and Hierarchy

Theory, Chapter 5

theory-05-latent-structure.Rmd

The gap between process and observation

Vegetation cover as recorded in a plot is not the same thing as the ecological process that generates it. The recorded value is a constrained, discretised, and bounded summary of something more fundamental: the capacity of a species to occupy space under the conditions present at that location.

This distinction matters. The ecological quantity of interest—call it suitability, intensity, or potential—is not inherently bounded between zero and one. It is not inherently compositional. It does not sum to one across species because ecology demands it. These constraints arise from the act of measurement: we observe cover within a finite plot, so the observed values must partition that plot.

The previous chapters established that constraints, dependence, and zeros are unavoidable features of observed cover data. This chapter argues that these features belong to the observation process, not to the underlying ecological quantities. Modelling observed values directly conflates process and measurement. Separating them requires latent structure.

Why direct modelling fails

Consider attempting to model observed cover proportions as the primary process. The model must:

  1. Respect the simplex constraint (values non-negative, summing to one).
  2. Allow exact zeros with positive probability.
  3. Represent dependence among components that is partly geometric and partly ecological.
  4. Accommodate variation that differs in character across species.

No single distribution on the simplex accomplishes all of this. Chapter 3 established that admissible distributions on the simplex have restricted covariance structures. Chapter 4 established that continuous distributions cannot represent exact zeros. Attempting to build a model that does everything at the observation level leads to either: (a) a model that violates the constraints, (b) a model that cannot represent zeros, or (c) a model with an impoverished dependence structure.

The problem is not that we lack sufficiently flexible distributions. The problem is that we are asking one layer to do too much. The simplex constraint, the zero structure, and the ecological variation are distinct phenomena. Collapsing them into a single distributional choice forces compromises that distort what the model represents.

What latent variables accomplish

A latent variable is an unobserved quantity that mediates between the process of interest and the data. In the context of cover data, latent variables serve a specific structural role: they carry ecological variation in an unconstrained space, before the observation process imposes constraints.

Consider a latent quantity for each species kk at each plot—call it an intensity, a suitability, or simply a latent value. The exact parameterisation and interpretation will be specified in later chapters. What matters here is the structural role: this latent quantity represents the species’ tendency to occupy space under the conditions present, before the observation process imposes constraints.

The latent values are not bounded. They are not required to sum to anything across species. They can be modelled with familiar tools: Gaussian distributions, linear predictors, covariance structures that encode ecological similarity or spatial proximity.

The observed cover proportions are then generated from these latent intensities through a mapping that imposes the simplex constraint and determines presence or absence. The constraints that seemed burdensome at the observation level become natural consequences of the mapping. They are not forced onto the model; they emerge from structure.

This separation clarifies what each part of the model represents:

  • Latent layer: Ecological variation, species-specific effects, environmental responses. Modelled in unconstrained space with flexible dependence.
  • Observation layer: The constraint that cover must sum to one, the discretisation into presence/absence, the measurement of proportions within a bounded plot.

The observed data are projections of latent structure through an observation process. The projection imposes constraints. The latent structure is where ecological inference happens.

Hierarchy as logical necessity

The term “hierarchical model” sometimes suggests an optional elaboration—a way to add complexity when simpler models fail. For constrained intensity data, this framing is backwards. Hierarchy is not added to a simpler model. It is what remains when we refuse to conflate distinct sources of variation.

The structure can be written schematically as a factorisation of the joint distribution:

p(data,latent)=p(data∣latent)×p(latent) p(\text{data}, \text{latent}) = p(\text{data} \mid \text{latent}) \times p(\text{latent})

The first term, p(data∣latent)p(\text{data} \mid \text{latent}), is the observation model. It describes how latent intensities become observed proportions. This is where the simplex constraint lives. This is where zeros are generated. This is where the compositional structure is imposed.

The second term, p(latent)p(\text{latent}), is the process model. It describes how latent intensities vary across species, plots, and conditions. This is where ecological covariance belongs. This is where environmental predictors enter. This is where species-level parameters are specified.

The factorisation is not a modelling convenience. It reflects the structure of the problem. Observed cover data are conditionally independent given the latent intensities: once we know the underlying ecological state, the observation process is determined. The dependence among observations arises from shared latent structure, not from direct connections among observed values.

Zeros revisited

Chapter 4 established that zeros require discrete structure to represent exactly. In a hierarchical view, this structure has a natural home.

The latent intensity λk\lambda_k for a species can be positive, indicating some capacity to occupy space, or it can be such that the species has zero probability of presence. The observation model then includes a presence indicator: given the latent intensity, is the species present in this plot? If yes, what proportion of space does it occupy?

This two-stage structure—presence given latent intensity, then allocation given presence—respects the compositional constraint while placing probability mass exactly at zero. The zeros are not approximations. They are outcomes of a discrete process that operates on latent quantities.

Importantly, presence and allocation are not modelled independently across species. The latent intensities are correlated. The presence indicators depend on these correlated intensities. The allocation among present species is constrained to sum to one minus the absent species’ share. The hierarchy couples these components without forcing a single distribution to represent everything.

What dependence means in this view

Chapter 2 established that compositional dependence is geometric and unavoidable. Chapter 3 showed that different distributions on the simplex encode different dependence assumptions. In a hierarchical view, these facts find their proper place.

The observed dependence among cover proportions arises from two sources:

  1. Latent covariance: Species with similar ecological requirements will have correlated latent intensities. This is the ecological part of dependence—the part we want to learn about.

  2. Constraint-induced dependence: Even if latent intensities were independent, observed proportions would be dependent because they must sum to one. This is the geometric part—the part that is structurally guaranteed.

Direct modelling of observed proportions conflates these sources. The Dirichlet, for instance, imposes a specific mixture of geometric and ecological dependence that cannot be disentangled. The logistic-normal allows more flexible dependence but only among present species.

In a hierarchical model, the sources are separated. Latent covariance encodes ecological dependence. The observation model encodes geometric dependence. Inference can target the latent covariance, which represents the scientifically interesting structure, rather than the observed covariance, which mixes signal with constraint.

Conditional independence and its implications

A key feature of hierarchical structure is conditional independence. Given the latent intensities, the observed cover values are generated through a process that does not require further connections among plots or among species beyond what the latent layer provides.

This does not mean observations are independent. It means their dependence is mediated. Two plots with similar observed cover have similar observations because they have similar latent structure, not because one plot’s cover directly influences another’s.

Conditional independence has practical implications:

  • The likelihood factorises into terms that depend on individual observations given their latent values.
  • Complex dependence structures are built into the latent layer, not the observation layer.
  • The observation model can be relatively simple—a mapping from latent intensities to proportions—while the process model carries the ecological complexity.

This is not a simplification for computational convenience. It is a statement about how the world works: observations are conditionally independent because the data-generating process goes through latent ecological states.

What hierarchy does not do

Introducing latent structure does not solve all problems. It clarifies structure but does not guarantee identifiability. If two different latent configurations produce the same distribution of observed data, the data cannot distinguish them.

For compositional data with zeros, identifiability is a genuine concern. When most species are absent from most plots, the latent values for absent species are weakly informed by the data. We observe that the species is absent, but many latent configurations are consistent with absence. The data constrain the latent values to be “low enough” to produce absence, but do not pinpoint them precisely.

Similarly, the allocation of cover among present species provides information about relative latent values, but the absolute scale may be poorly determined. The mapping from latent values to observed proportions involves normalisation, which can absorb shifts in the overall level of latent values.

A hierarchical view does not eliminate these limitations. It makes them explicit. The latent layer is partly identified by the data (through observed presences and cover values) and partly regularised by structure (through the process model and any priors). What the data cannot tell us, the model cannot recover—regardless of how it is parameterised. The role of structural assumptions and priors is to provide coherent behaviour in weakly identified regions, not to fabricate information.

This is a feature, not a bug. A model that obscures identifiability problems is harder to diagnose than one that exposes them. Hierarchical structure exposes them by separating what is observed from what is inferred.

Summary

The constraints, dependence, and zeros of cover data are features of observation, not of the underlying ecological process. Modelling observations directly requires a single distributional family to represent all of these features simultaneously. No such family exists that is both admissible and flexible.

The alternative is to separate process from observation through latent structure. Latent intensities carry ecological variation in an unconstrained space. The observation model maps these intensities to constrained proportions, imposing the simplex structure and generating zeros through a discrete mechanism.

This hierarchy is not a modelling convenience. It is the structure that remains when we take the constraints seriously. The observed data are projections of latent ecological states. The projections are constrained; the states are not. Inference about ecology operates on the latent layer.

This chapter establishes only that the structure is necessary. A framework that operates directly on observed proportions, without acknowledging latent mediation, has not separated process from measurement. It has conflated them.
